summary.text: A 72-year-old right-handed man with diabetes mellitus had a reverse shoulder arthroplasty for cuff tear arthropathy of the right shoulder at another institution. He later developed shoulder pain, swelling, redness and purulent discharge with a fistula, was diagnosed with infection, and underwent debridement with insert exchange and systemic antibiotics, but infection control remained unsuccessful and he was referred.

On admission he was afebrile with a sinus tract and continuous purulent drainage and a mild increase in inflammatory response. Joint aspiration grew ESBL-producing Klebsiella oxytoca and Staphylococcus aureus, both aminoglycoside susceptible. Radiographs showed osteolysis around the humeral component and MRI showed fluid collection and fistula formation. Chronic periprosthetic joint infection was diagnosed as definite by ICM criteria.

He underwent one-stage revision with removal of all components, extensive debridement, irrigation and exchange to a new reverse shoulder system. Gentamicin continuous local antibiotic perfusion with negative pressure wound therapy was given for 14 days, with serum gentamicin trough and renal monitoring, followed by about six weeks of intravenous and oral antibiotics. Intraoperative cultures revealed bacteria similar to the preoperative aspirate.

The postoperative course was uneventful with infection signs resolving. At one year he was pain-free with no recurrence of infection and no antibiotics; forward flexion was 100 degrees, abduction 90 degrees, external rotation 10 degrees, internal rotation to the sacrum, and JOA score 69 compared with 38 before revision. Radiographs showed stable fixation at one month and one year, and no clinical signs of toxicity were observed.

caption_evidence.quote:
Figure 3
Postoperative management with continuous local antibiotic perfusion (CLAP).A negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT) system combined with continuous local antibiotic perfusion using gentamicin (60 mg/50 mL at 2 mL/h) was applied. NPWT was set to continuous negative pressure, and the dressing was changed every two to three days. The inflow catheter was inserted into the glenohumeral joint space, and the outflow catheter was incorporated into the NPWT foam dressing. The catheters and tubing were secured with sutures and an additional adhesive drape to prevent leaks and maintain a closed circuit, increasing local antibiotic concentrations at the surgical site while minimizing systemic exposure.
